opus-4-8: Opus paints a gorgeous sunset and then interrupts it with a DOM modal every ninety seconds — nothing says 1986 arcade like filling out a form to turn left.
The spec asked for collisions and spins; Opus interpreted both as a gentle sideways apology.
Its city towers re-roll their window lights every single frame, which is either a rendering bug or the world's fastest landlord.
Five endings and no route map — you discover where you're going the way you discover roadworks.
The road fades romantically into fog while palm trees materialize out of thin air, because fogging sprites was apparently someone else's job.
The soundtrack stops dead at every fork so you can contemplate your route in awkward silence.
Traffic never changes lanes; the entire highway has tenure.
1,417 lines is a lovely haiku, but this contest called for a novel.
The scarf flutter on the passenger is genuinely charming, which makes it stranger that the car cannot spin, skid, or do anything else a car does.
Beautiful warm palette, shame the route selection UI was borrowed from a tax filing portal.
gpt-5-5: The brief said warm 1980s sunset; GPT 5.5 delivered a Windows default wallpaper.
The fork screen pauses the timer indefinitely — less a route choice, more a save state.
The end screen proudly reports PASSES: 0 every run, which is at least honest about its stat tracking.
No fog anywhere, so the scenery pops in at the horizon like it missed its cue.
The soundtrack is one brave square wave doing its very best.
Its stages loop with modulo arithmetic, making déjà vu a core game mechanic.
Its idea of golden hour is hex code #1188f2.
The traffic AI genuinely drifts between lanes — the cars received more art direction than the sky.
Checkpoints are invisible distance triggers; you celebrate by squinting at the timer.
It renders scanlines over a palette that has never once seen a CRT.
gpt-5-4: Six HUD readouts plus a live status joke ticker — the road is a supporting character in its own racing game.
The title screen advertises eight endings; the code politely ships four.
There is technically music, at gain 0.01, performing nightly for an audience of nobody.
The car is hard-coded at 140 pixels wide: a monster truck on a phone, a Hot Wheels on a monitor.
It has the only route map in the field and rebuilds it from scratch every time an overlay opens.
Every stage ends in a full-stop modal, because nothing sustains adrenaline like reading.
3,093 lines and the frame clamp still turns lag into a slow-motion replay.
Hesitate at a fork and it chooses for you — helicopter parenting as game design.
The status bar heckles you mid-race, which is bold for a game with no fog and pop-in scenery.
It calls the checkpoint screen a tour, which is accurate, because the game keeps stopping to rest.
gpt-5-4-mini: 3,965 lines of code and the canvas still gets squashed into funhouse-mirror proportions on a phone.
Hold the gas and the game gently decays you back to the chapter's speed target — an arcade racer with a hall monitor.
Brake while steering above speed 140 and you spin instantly; the punishment for using both pedals is the tutorial.
It declares SAVE_KEY and never uses it — even the constants have abandonment issues.
Ten chapters, weather, and a damage model, all viewed through a stretched 960 by 540 letterbox.
Hesitate at a fork and it auto-picks option one, which is also how it approached its rendering architecture.
The audio bus architecture is genuinely superb, wasted on a renderer that squashes the sunset into an ellipse.
A setInterval pokes the DOM every 500 milliseconds like it is refreshing its email.
Top speed is 240 but the game only lets you borrow it briefly, with interest.
It seats two passengers this time — witnesses to the aspect ratio.
